entries.title: How Massive Is Elon Musk’s Trillion-Dollar Fortune? Spend It Yourself
entries.summary: WIRED has partnered with Neal Agarwal of Neal.fun to create a visualization of Elon Musk’s massive wealth. Here’s how it came together.
entries.content:
On any given day, Elon Musk is worth about a trillion dollars. This does not mean that he has a trillion dollar bills sitting in an old-timey vault in a dusty basement somewhere; his wealth is mostly tied up in shares of SpaceX and Tesla. But if he were to cash those out, sell Neuralink and the Boring Company, and scrounge together some extra change, his checking account would hit 13 digits.

“Trillionaire” is an easy enough word to say. It’s fun, even! Rolls off the tongue. But research has shown that the human brain has a very hard time comprehending the actual size and scope of large numbers. “Trillion” sounds like a short hop from “billion,” after all, even though it is in fact 1,000 times bigger. And even if you are somehow able to wrap your mind around that immense scale, it still feels abstract, no matter how many times you compare it to the area of Central Park or the weight of a fleet of trucks. Maybe a better way to visualize a trillion dollars, then, is through what you can actually buy with it.

WIRED has partnered with Neal Agarwal, the proprietor of the consistently delightful website Neal.fun, to do just that. Spend Elon Musk’s Money is a new visualization that lets you, well, spend Elon Musk’s money, on anything from Big Macs to aircraft carriers to the Las Vegas Sphere. It keeps a tally as you go, so you can actually see how far a trillion dollars gets you these days, and it shows the items you’ve bought in a physical space.

WIRED spoke with Agarwal about this new project, why it feels so relevant now, and the state of building things on the web. You can read that interview below, and waste a few hours on Spend Elon Musk’s money right here.

This interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

WIRED: I’ve known about Neal.fun for a long time, I’m a big fan. But describe it for someone who’s never been there.

Neal Agarwal: I never wanted to constrain the site to one thing, so it ended up being almost like a journal at this point. I’ve been running it since I was 19, and it’s kind of a catalog of everything I’m interested in: visualizations, science, weird game mechanics. For me, it’s mostly an exploration of what you can do with a website.

Why is that important to you, the idea of exploring what a website is and means? If there’s one thing I know about you it’s that you love the web.

Very much so. I grew up on the web; I was 8 years old on forums. I probably spent more time in Club Penguin than any real-world walls. I’m definitely a child of the web, and it’s interesting that I’m around the same age as it. It’s a privilege. Painters are working in a medium that’s a thousand years older, a million years older, so a lot of things have already been found out, been fleshed out. But on the web there’s so much that we haven’t figured out yet. I think there’s still a lot of new stuff to discover, and that’s really interesting to me.

I think every medium has distinct things you can do with it. You can turn a book into a movie but it’s not quite the same. There are some things a book is always going to be better at, and vice versa. I think that’s true of the web too. This visualization we’re working on, you can’t print it in a newspaper.

I suspect people might be familiar with some of your individual projects, if not your site itself. To list some off that are huge in my household: The Password Game, Space Elevator, The Deep Sea, Infinite Craft. When something goes viral, as so many of these have, what’s it like on your end? Is it almost boring now to see things blow up?

I think each project has been very different. The ones that excite me the most now are where a lot of people play it and start doing things with it that I did not expect or intend. Within a few days of Infinite Craft launching, people started crafting Japanese words within the game. And they crafted enough Japanese words that they could play the whole game in Japanese. I’ve never released a game before where they unlocked a language.

I had another one called Internet Road Trip; it’s like a simulated road trip but through Google Street View. A Discord formed around that, and people started backseat driving and arguing over which city to go to next, should they make a pit stop here so they can see this monument. People started birdwatching within that game. All these emergent things started happening, and I think the web is really good at that, too. It’s really good at forming communities out of the silliest things, which I find really exciting.

There’s also this contrast with a more closed-off app environment; you don’t really work in apps as a medium.

When I was a teenager I did make some apps, but I always really disliked that Apple and Google had to approve what I could put in them, and you have to wait a week for approval, and if they don’t like your app you have no recourse. So just the idea of having a homepage where it’s like, this is my homepage. Nobody can tell me what to do with it. I can put whatever I want.

We should talk about this visualization, Spend Elon Musk’s Money. It’s sort of a sequel to Spend Bill Gates’ Money, which was one of your first projects, right?

That actually launched with the website itself. I just wanted to showcase how much $100 billion was, which I guess now seems like a little amount of money compared to the trillion we’re working with.

It’s almost quaint, right? The premise is you’ve got a $100 billion counter and a bunch of things you can buy with prices attached to them: a Big Mac, flip-flops, a lobster dinner, a year of Netflix, all the way up to things like a diamond ring, a Ferrari, a McDonald’s franchise, and then up again to the Mona Lisa. And you just keep trying to add it up. What was the response to that game when it first launched?

It was one of the biggest things I’ve launched, and it was really nice to see that the point got across. People understood that this is a way to visualize wealth that isn’t just graphs and bar charts. The game kept finding a new audience over and over again; it was an idea that kept being interesting to people.

And then we come to 2026, and we have a trillionaire in the world, and it felt like maybe the right time to revisit.

Yeah, I think so. There’s a lot more you can do to visualize that, too. That’s why this one is 3D. I think one thing with Spend Bill Gates’ money is, yeah, you can buy 10,000 cars, but it’s still a number on a screen. With Spend Elon Musk’s Money, I want you to see the cars you’re buying on a screen. The amount of physical stuff you can buy—it is an empire.

One thing that I certainly have a hard time with, and I think most people do, is really wrapping your head around what a trillion is. There’s been research that humans are really bad at processing how big the jumps are even from 1 billion to 2 billion, much less getting up to a trillion. Our brains just break.

I think that’s one thing the web is actually really good at, is that you have infinite space. You can visualize these numbers in ways that you can’t do in the physical world. Even for my project The Deep Sea, it’s a 1:1 of the ocean. If you wanted to print that out on paper, it would be a mile long, but on the web you can just keep scrolling and scrolling. So it’s kind of fun to have this infinite scroll mechanic to visualize these huge numbers.

Some of the items carry over from Spend Bill Gates Money, some are different. How did you think about the best mix of options to give people?

This time I was going for more tangible things, so you can visualize it. It’s honestly hard to think of items; once you get to $100 million, there are only so many things out on the market that you can buy. So we have the Las Vegas Sphere in there, and aircraft carriers.

After a point it’s kind of interesting that you’re like, OK, I could buy 1,000 more tanks, what would that really get me? Part of the fun of this one is just the futility of it. At a certain point, what more could a person need?

For sure. I just bought 1,000 monster trucks, and I still have $999,650,000 left.

There were a few different ideas. One is if you had a trillion dollars and just had a stack of money, and as you spend it you see the trillion dollars go down, but it’s actually pretty hard to render a trillion dollars in bills on the page.

I had thoughts of more abstract things. Once you get to a trillion dollars you’re really buying power, so how many companies you could buy or how much influence you have. But for most people, that’s a harder way to visualize things than, like, oh, that is a million racehorses I just bought.

Did you run into any technical challenges building this?

Initially I wanted everything to be 3D models on the site. But if you try to get your laptop to render a million monster trucks, it’s just going to freeze. So I had to do a lot of trickery to get this 3D effect without actually using 3D models.

It doesn’t just tell us about Elon Musk, it tells us about the things we’re buying. I looked back at the original Spend Bill Gates’ Money, and the Big Mac was $2. It’s $6 now. For anything where there’s a direct parallel, you’ve captured a real price jump.

It’s very inflation-adjusted. Which is crazy, because it’s only been six or seven years. If anyone has any recommendations about other items we should add to this, just let me know.

entries.title: Life Is Asymmetric. The Scientists Who Figured Out Why Won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry
entries.summary: Henri Kagan and Kensō Soai designed chemical reactions producing only one of the two mirror-image forms of a molecule—an important finding for the synthesis of pharmaceuticals and other biological substances.
entries.content:
The 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Henri Kagan and Kensō Soai for discovering a solution to the enigma of nature’s chemical asymmetry, a finding that opened up new avenues for manipulating the reactions used in manufacturing pharmaceuticals and other materials.

Some molecules are chiral, meaning a molecule has two forms that are mirror images of each other but not identical, like your left and right hand. One of the most mysterious chemical phenomena in biology is that living organisms contain almost exclusively one of the two forms. This is known as homochirality.

Both versions of the molecules—each called an enantiomer—have similar physical properties but can behave differently. The Nobel Committee used a simple analogy to explain this: A locksmith can create two mirror-image keys, but “only one of them fits the lock—and the lock can be damaged if your customers try to unlock it with the other key.”

In the development of new drugs that use, for example, amino acids or sugar molecules as a basis, homochirality poses a problem: While one of the enantiomers of these chiral molecules produces the desired therapeutic effect, the other can cause unnecessary and, at times, harmful side effects. Scientists can’t always easily control which version of the molecule they get out of their synthesis.

The discovery of chiral molecules dates back to the time of Pasteur, who found two enantiomers that reacted very differently when exposed to bacteria. Since then, various researchers have attempted to replicate homochirality in the laboratory with the goal of understanding its spontaneous origin and applying this knowledge to the design of controlled reactions for various purposes. However, early experiments yielded equal amounts of the two variants, failing to reproduce the selectivity observed in nature.

At the beginning of the last century, the German chemist Willy Marckwald designed an asymmetric reaction capable of producing a slightly greater amount of one of the two versions. He achieved this using a chiral catalyst—a substance that facilitates a chemical reaction without being consumed and favors the formation of one of the enantiomers. The ratio between the two variants, however, only changed a little.

Later, in 1953, theoretical physicist Charles Frank proposed a mathematical model that outlined three conditions for reproducing homochirality. First, there must be an asymmetric reaction capable of favoring one of the two versions; that imbalance has to be amplified; and the reaction itself has to produce the catalyst that drives it. This last characteristic is called autocatalysis and generates a kind of positive feedback loop, in which a small initial advantage can cause one of the variants to assemble at an ever-faster rate until it dominates the reaction.

This framework formed the basis of Henri Kagan’s research. Beginning in the early 1980s, he focused on refining asymmetric reactions through a detailed study of the catalyst. At that time, scientists typically used catalysts consisting of a metal atom that acted as the reaction’s driving force and a chiral substance that ensured the process was asymmetric. They assumed that if they used a mixture containing equal amounts of the two versions of that chiral molecule, the result would also be a balanced mixture.

Kagan began to question that idea. He realized that the metal atom likely did not interact with just one enantiomer but with both at the same time. This meant that, by mixing versions A and B, three different combinations could form: A-A, B-B, and B-A. The first two would produce molecules that were mirror images of each other. But the A-B combination could behave differently during the reaction.

The A-B combination, the scientist discovered, could slow down the reaction, indirectly favoring the formation of one of the two versions of the final molecule. The phenomenon was called the “nonlinear effect” and represented a new way to manipulate chemical reactions.

“In addition to their practical interest, nonlinear effects are a very valuable tool for studying reaction mechanisms and the nature of catalytically active species,” explained José María Andrés García, a professor in the Department of Organic Chemistry at the University of Valladolid, in a statement reported by SMC Spain.

Inspired by Kagan’s findings, Kensō Soai sought to create a reaction in which the product itself would act as a catalyst and help produce more molecules identical to itself—one of those theoretical conditions for the homochirality. He conducted a test with a substance known as 5-pyrimidylalkanol. At the beginning of the experiment, one version was just 2 percent more abundant than the other version of the molecule. By the end of the reaction, that advantage had jumped to 87 percent.

In the years that followed, Soai worked toward achieving reactions that resulted in the near-absolute purity of one enantiomer, replicating the molecular state inside living organisms. Finally, in 2003, he engineered a reaction in which the starting substances had no defined orientation, but as they reacted, a slightly greater amount of one enantiomer appeared by chance. That tiny difference then produced many more molecules of the same variant. Gradually, that form came to dominate the reaction, accounting for up to 99.99 percent of the final product.

In other words, the reaction formed only one of the two possible enantiomers. As the Nobel Committee stated, “Other than life itself, no one had previously achieved this feat.”

This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

entries.title: Best Reusable Water Bottles of 2026, Tested by WIRED
entries.summary: We dropped them, tossed them in bags, and cleaned their fiddly lids. Here are the ones we recommend.
entries.content:
Reusable water bottles are a matter of personal taste, and WIRED reviewers have strong opinions on which jug reigns supreme. We’ve spent years testing, sipping, and spilling our way through the best water bottles to round up our favorites.

A note to remember: You only need one reusable bottle (though I won’t judge if you rotate between two). More than that defeats the environmental purpose of purchasing a reusable bottle in the first place. Also, be aware that some insulated bottles use lead solder. We’ve removed those from our list. We have some standards, after all.

Does your water need to be even cleaner? Check out our guide to the Best Backpacking Water Filters. Then get one of our Best Travel Mugs or Best Tote Bags.

Updated October 2026: We’ve added the Owala FreeSip Sway and Path Water Bottle as picks and the Bentgo Lift Chug as an honorable mention. We also moved the Owala FreeSip Twist to honorable mentions and ensured up-to-date prices and information throughout.

Featured in this Article

A PSA on Lead

Some water bottle companies use lead soldering to manufacture their vacuum-sealed bottles. The Stanley Quencher tumbler is one of them. No amount of lead exposure is safe, but it poses particular risk for children and pregnant people. The company has confirmed that some pellets used to seal the bottom of the cup use lead, but unless you remove or damage the bottom of the cup, the lead will not come into contact with your beverage or skin.

The risk of exposure might be very low, but it should be zero. Given that many brands practice lead-free manufacturing, we think the proximity to exposure is unnecessary.

Best Overall

A longtime favorite of outdoorsy folks and anyone else who wants a water bottle that’s not easily damaged, Hydro Flask has staying power. That may be due in part to its customization capability: Pick your preferred type of bottle, cap, and color, and if you buy from Hydro Flask, you can also engrave many styles. You can choose one color for the bottle, another for the lid, and depending on those choices, yet another for the strap or straw. —Boutayna Chokrane

Best for Straw Lovers

Owala perfected its FreeSip design with the Sway, which includes familiar features of other bottles in the line, like fun colors, triple-layer insulation, and a multifunctional mouthpiece that lets you sip through its straw or tilt the bottle upward to swig through its spout. Details that lift the Sway above its FreeSip cousins include its convenient top-carry handle that’s easy to hold, contoured side edges that let you get a comfortable grip while you drink, and its attached push-button opening with a locking mechanism that both lets you drink one-handed and also saves you from unfortunate spills.

Its materials are durable, it comes in four sizes (the 30-ounce option is plenty big for me without being too cumbersome), and the lid is dishwasher-safe. Even so, because the lid has a lot of edges and ridges where gunk can get trapped, I like to clean it by hand, which is a bit of a pain.

The wider top lid screws off completely, letting you add ice or easily pour in any other beverage, but it’s important to close it tightly before throwing it in your bag. The same warning applies to ensuring you’ve toggled on the mouthpiece lock. While the Sway is indeed leakproof when used as directed, the bottle is ripe for user-error spills, as I’ve learned the hard way. But if you look over to your passenger seat while you’re driving and see water pooling around your bottle because you forgot to close it correctly, at least you can snatch it up easily and plop it into a cup holder—a win that some other FreeSip models don’t offer. —Alexis Berger

Best BPA-Free Plastic

Today’s youths love their wide-leg jeans and Nirvana T-shirts, but ask any ’90s kid, and they’ll tell you that the look is incomplete without the water bottle of our times: the classic Nalgene. Originally made of bulletproof (and BPA-rich) Lexan, the Nalgene was the original name-brand water bottle, a symbol of good taste and outdoorsy vibes to be toted between Planet Hollywood and Blockbuster. The Nalgene had a complete chokehold on the premillennial culture, propping up water at a time when Surge and Josta were at such ready supply that human beings may well have stopped consuming plain water entirely were it not for the Nalgene. The brand has since replaced the chemical plastic with modern materials like Tritan, which is BPA-free and made of half-recycled plastic, but it otherwise remains the same: a perfect bottle, carrying a reasonable supply of fluid for the day with a secure screw-top lid, handy measurement lines, and a wide mouth for ice cubes and easy cleaning—unlike the bacteria-teeming straws on those adult sippy cups. —Martin Cizmar

Size Options (ounces) 32
Lids Available Wide Screw Cap (included)
Dishwasher-Safe Yes

Best Self-Cleaning

The Larq bottle eases all my germaphobic concerns with reusable water bottles. It uses a nontoxic UV-C LED light in the lid to sterilize the water every two hours (or more often, if prompted), which reduces funky odors and bacterial buildup. It’s double-insulated, made from BPA-free stainless steel, and a full charge lasts up to three weeks. Plus, the app lets you track your water-intake objectives—though honestly, it didn’t inspire me to drink more.

The company also sells the PureVis 2, but the filter is a hassle. It tends to slip into the bottle when full, and it chokes the water flow, which isn’t ideal when you’re wheezing in the middle of a hot yoga class. The filter also eats up a lot of space inside the bottle, so you’re left with less water than you’d think, and the mouthpiece is not the easiest to clean. So, while I love the idea of better-tasting drinking water, I just prefer its OG, filter-free version. —Boutayna Chokrane

Best Filter

The Brita bottle is a good portable filtering option for folks who are particular about the taste and smell of their H2O. This hard-sided plastic bottle is BPA-free, Water Quality Association (WQA)-certified, and available in a range of vibrant colors. The activated carbon block filter effectively reduces chlorine and other impurities. However, I find the straw difficult to clean, which can be a hassle. Also, you’ll need to replace the filter either every two months or after it purifies 40 gallons (whichever occurs first). Despite these drawbacks, it’s a great choice for tap water without a chlorine taste, and at an affordable price. —Boutayna Chokrane

Size Options (ounces) 26
Lids Available Push-Button Lid (Included)
Dishwasher-Safe Yes. Remove the filter and place all plastic components, including the bottle and lid, in the top rack only.

Best Tumbler

I love this tumbler because the built-in straw stays tucked away, so I don’t need to buy a separate straw cover that I’ll immediately lose. The lid has a push-button open with a lock, so I don’t hesitate to toss it in a bag, which is a luxury you don’t get with most tumblers. It’s also double-threaded for lefties and righties, and the tapered base fits into most cup holders. Like all Owala bottles, it’s BPA-, lead-, and phthalate-free.

A few caveats about the tumbler: The push-button lid doesn’t jam as much as the original FreeSip, but I have been caught in the splash zone, so open with caution. Also, I dropped it on my pinky toe once, and I’m 90 percent sure I have a hairline fracture. Handle this one with care. —Boutayna Chokrane

Lids Available FreeSip Tumbler Lid (included)
Dishwasher-Safe Dishwasher-safe lid and hand-washable cup.

Best Sustainable

Though the Ocean Bottle is one of the smallest water bottles I own, it’s still the one I find myself grabbing most frequently for hikes and short trips. Made of 90 percent recycled stainless steel, it comes in 10-plus colors, is BPA-free, and is available in 17-oz (the size I have), 26-oz, and 34-oz options. It features a screw-cap lid, and the top also screws off about a quarter of the way down for easy filling or adding ice. You can also remove both segments at once and turn them upside down to transform the bottle into a leakproof cup. It’s also got a handy silicone carry loop. It’s pricey, but at least you won’t need to feel guilty about someday adding to the landfill graveyard of out-of-trend Stanleys and Hydro Flasks—for each bottle sold, Ocean Bottle funds the collection of 25 pounds of ocean-bound plastic. —Kat Merck

Best Recyclable

If you have kids who are constantly losing their water bottle—or, like mine, refused for a while to carry a water bottle because they knew for a fact they would lose it—Path might be a good solution. These lightweight, refillable aluminum bottles are around $5 each and come pre-filled with still, sparkling, flavored, or alkaline water. The bottles themselves come in solid or ombre colors, seasonal patterns, or collabs like the just-released state collection. Refill them until they get lost or dented to oblivion (there’s even a spot on the bottle to mark how many times it’s refilled), then recycle it and grab a new one. Note that they are easily dinged up, so make sure your kid has a sufficiently padded lunchbox to protect it. Also, some kids with sensory needs may balk at the slightly metallic taste once they’re refilled. —Kat Merck

More Bottles to Consider

Owala FreeSip Twist for $30: I now understand the hype around Owala’s FreeSip: It’s insulated, so the cold water stays icy all day, even during Midwest summers. Its innovative design caters to the majority; you can sip from either the built-in straw or the chug spout. And the lid is dishwasher-safe for easy cleaning, though I prefer hand-washing for extra care. The color options are another highlight, with various vibrant combinations available to suit any style. I do prefer the twist-cap version for daily use over the classic. I’ve noticed the latter’s push-button lock is a bit flimsy and tends to jam. But while I trust a twist cap for preventing spillage, it’s easier to lose than an attached lid, like what you get with top-pick FreeSip Sway. —Boutayna Chokrane

Bentgo Lift Chug Lid for $30: I assumed I wasn’t going to like this water bottle because, to me, its ring handle that sits atop the mouthpiece conjures an unappetizing toilet donut. But it turns out the handle is comfortable to hold and quite functional as a locking mechanism for the bottle. The push-button lid beneath the handle also works nicely. Sipping is a bit awkward—I had to do it sideways so my nose didn’t hit the plastic piece connecting the ring handle to the lid. I’m almost willing to overlook that detail because the triple-layer insulation of the BPA- and PFAS-free material works well to keep water cold, the wide-mouth opening offers welcome flexibility for filling and cleaning the bottle, it’s dishwasher-safe, and the color options are nice; however, the bottle is too wide for a standard cup holder, and that’s a tough swig to swallow. —Alexis Berger

Fellow Carter Carry Water Bottle for $45: Fellow’s insulated water bottle is relatively tall and thin, with a squared metal carry loop that comfortably fits three fingers. The Carter holds temps for several hours (the brand claims the bottle can keep water cold for 24 hours, but mine was at room temperature by the end of a long day). What I really like about this bottle, though, is actually drinking from it. The Carter has a slightly tapered lip like a wine glass, which helps avoid spillage, and the ceramic interior coating means that the water coming out of the bottle tastes just like it did going in. If you like the minimalist look and need an insulated bottle that’s actually pleasant to sip from, the Carter delivers. —Martin Cizmar

Takeya Glow-in-the-Dark Sport Kids Bottle for $30: Takeya promises to “make hydration exciting” with its glow-in-the-dark bottle, so it’s important to point out that it’s just the band that glows, not the neon paint splatters. Nevertheless, this is a sturdy triple-insulated bottle with a big carry handle for clumsy or distracted little hands. The slim 18-oz size also fits in the side pocket of my two kids’ school backpacks. However, my 8-year-old is annoyed by the fact that the straw leaks air and whistles when he drinks. —Adrienne So

Created Co. Wander Bottle (26 ounces) for $36: I like that the Wander Bottle is created with 18/8 insulated stainless steel, but because the spout is made of BPA-free plastic, my water doesn’t taste like metal. The simple two-piece design makes for easy hand-washing, and the wide carry handle is comfortable to hold during hikes or other on-the-go situations. —Boutayna Chokrane

Yeti Yonder Water Bottle with Yonder Tether Cap for $54: Stainless steel water bottles keep drinks cold, but sometimes they feel like you’re lugging around a dumbbell. If you travel a lot or have little kids who maybe don’t need to knock themselves out with a heavy-duty Stanley, you might want something lighter (and safer). Former WIRED editor Adrienne So calls the 25-ounce Yeti Yonder her emotional support water bottle. It’s lightweight, made from 50 percent recycled plastic, and BPA-free. The cap is also well-designed to prevent spills if you’re a chugger. So’s bottle has survived many drops and playground tumbles without a scratch. But if you somehow do manage to damage it, it’s covered by a five-year warranty. Bonus: It’s dishwasher-safe. —Boutayna Chokrane

Dometic Insulated Chug Bottle for $45: The lids to these insulated bottles are interchangeable with plenty of accessories, like a tea infuser and handle (sold separately), for a customizable experience. The bottle kept ice intact for days in my tests; the only thing I didn’t like over time is that the straw (the bottom portion of which is metal) doesn’t reach all the way to the bottom on larger-size bottles, so you’re unable to access a fair amount of your drink. —Kat Merck

Klean Kanteen 32-oz TKWide Insulated Water Bottle with Twist Cap for $47: If you want one bottle to do it all, grab the Klean Kanteen TKWide. Its modular cap system lets you tailor hydration to your situation: Use the included twist cap with its built-in straw for everyday sipping, swap the Chug Cap for fast gulps during workouts, or screw on the Loop Cap for clipping to your backpack during hikes. Klean Kanteen even makes a Café Cap that turns your bottle into a spill-proof travel mug for your iced coffee. It’s made of 90 percent post-consumer recycled 18/8 stainless steel and is dishwasher safe, which is a huge bonus if you plan to use this thermos for protein shakes. Note: This bottle is for cold drinks only. —Boutayna Chokrane

Lifefactory 22-Ounce Glass Water Bottle with Active Flip Cap for $33: The active flip cap is convenient for quick sips, but you need to double-check that it’s closed before storing it. I’ve experienced a few spillage issues with this one. It comes in three sizes—the 12-ounce bottle is perfect for kids, but the largest is 22 ounces and could be bigger, especially for $35. Like most (if not all) of the glass bottles I recommend, this one also includes a protective silicone sleeve that provides a better grip and an extra layer of security. —Boutayna Chokrane

bkr Spiked Big Bottle 1L for $62: Glass water bottles are nontoxic and remain the cleanest, greenest choice. Bkr’s signature silicone protects the glass from shattering and also adds an edgy, grippy texture. It won’t dent or clang against surfaces, and if you drop it in a crowded room, it lands silently. —Boutayna Chokrane

Ello Cooper Twist Stainless Steel Water Bottle for $23: The Ello Cooper Twist Stainless Steel Water Bottle is vacuum-insulated, double-walled, and features a screw-on lid with a carry handle. The spout is a matter of personal preference, but I like the ceramic opening. If you prefer a chug cap, it’s a great option. —Boutayna Chokrane

Camelbak Eddy+ for $12: The Camelbak Eddy+ is a durable, lightweight, recycled plastic bottle with a straw lid. Adrienne So has had several of these for years. Just be sure to let the chew top air out daily because it’s prone to collecting mold if left damp. —Boutayna Chokrane

Pura Big Mouth Insulated Bottle for $47: Pura bottles are thin, light, and made entirely from stainless steel, so there’s no plastic or powder coating (which also means they may not withstand drops and bumps). They’re Made Safe Certified, meaning they’re made without 15,000 ingredients identified as harmful to human health and the environment. I don’t love the silicone lids, as they’re very thin and floppy, but you can unscrew the whole cap to sip right from the metal rim. —Boutayna Chokrane

Avoid These Bottles

Water.io Daily+ for $100: This is a bottle that tracks your sips and reminds you to drink, which sounds great, but in practice, is not the best. The battery life is short, lasting for two to three days, and it requires a proprietary charger. For $100, I’d expect more perks, like filtration or self-cleaning tech, but this bottle doesn’t deliver any of that. The water also picks up a metallic aftertaste that is far from refreshing. —Boutayna Chokrane

Air Up Water Bottle for $40: This bottle uses scented rings to try to trick your brain into thinking it isn’t drinking plain water. WIRED writer Boone Ashworth was unimpressed. It didn’t smell great, and you can’t use the bottle without one of those rings. The beauty of a reusable bottle is that you spend money once and get free water for years. Here, you have to keep buying refills. —Boutayna Chokrane

Frequently Asked Questions

How Much Water Do I Need?

The eight-glasses rule isn’t exactly accurate, but it’s a solid starting point. Since water intake is highly individualized (kind of like the bottle itself), it’s best to consult your doctor about the right amount for you. Several lifestyle factors can influence your hydration needs. If you’re active or sweat a lot, for example, you generally should increase your intake to make up for losses. Remember that while warmer temperatures can make us thirstier, drinking too much water can cause overhydration and sodium levels to drop to dangerous levels in a condition called hyponatremia.

Certain medications can lead to water retention, which is another reason why it can’t hurt to ask your physician about your personal ideal water intake during your next check-up. In the meantime, if you’re not thirsty and your urine is colorless or light yellow, you’re likely doing great, sweetie.

How Do Insulated Water Bottles Work?

An insulated water bottle consists of a double-wall construction with insulating materials that prevent heat transfer. Insulated bottles are heavier and can typically hold less water compared to their uninsulated counterparts, given similar exterior dimensions. However, the advantage is that insulated models are typically vacuum-sealed, allowing them to better maintain the temperature of the liquid inside for far longer periods.

Condensation is typical in non-insulated water bottles, where beads of water form on the exterior of the bottle. In this case, you may end up avoiding packing the bottle inside your bag to protect your personal items from your sweating water bottle.

Insulated bottles are made of stainless steel and other similar durable, damage-resistant materials. While they’re typically more expensive because of the higher-quality materials, advanced technology, and complex manufacturing process, insulated water bottles may also have a longer lifespan than their noninsulated counterparts. This can minimize waste and also save you money in the long run as a result of needing to buy fewer replacement water bottles over time.

For hiking and outdoor climbing trips, you may prefer uninsulated bottles because they are lighter weight, and your concern is likely having enough water rather than cold water. For most other purposes, insulated options work just fine.

How Should I Wash My Water Bottle?

Even if they never hold anything but water, bottles get gross. Mold can grow quickly, especially if you leave the cap on. Straws and mouthpieces accumulate bacteria, oils, and grime from your mouth, and any dirt and dust they pick up in your backpack.

Some bottles can go right in the dishwasher, but be sure to take everything fully apart first, like any silicone pieces that can trap bacteria. For lids that have more nooks and crannies, I recommend hand-washing by soaking them in soapy water and then scrubbing.

Get yourself a bottle brush and straw brush—many kits are available that include both. Even if you don’t use straws, the smaller brush is a helpful tool for getting into any crevices. There are special bottle-cleaning tablets around, but cleaning with regular dish soap works perfectly fine.

Plastic bottles tend to trap odors over time. You can fix this by putting a teaspoon of bleach and a teaspoon of baking soda in the bottle, filling it up with water, and letting it sit overnight. Rinse it out well the next day.

How We Test Reusable Water Bottles

We test every new water bottle for at least two weeks; however, most top picks are ones that members of the WIRED team have loved and carried for months or years. Here’s what we look for:

  • Design: First and foremost, we note which materials are used and evaluate whether they feel safe, sustainable, and durable. Because taste can also make or break a bottle, we evaluate whether materials retain odors or leave water tasting metallic or plasticky. We also consider how simple it is to replace parts like lids and straws.
  • Portability: We consider the size, weight, cup holder compatibility, and whether it’s designed with ergonomic features like a carry loop.
  • Durability: We drop bottles, toss them in totes, and use them daily to see if they dent, crack, or leak. We’ll also twist lids aggressively and test whether the hinges hold up after dozens of openings.
  • Ease of use and cleaning: Overall, we’ll judge how intuitive the bottle is to drink from and refill. Each bottle also goes through several rounds of hand-washing and dishwasher cycles (when safe) to evaluate how easy it is to clean and whether odors or stains linger.
  • Insulation: For insulated bottles, we’ll fill them with hot and ice-cold water for the advertised time to track how well they maintain temperature.

entries.title: WIRED’s Midterms Races to Watch
entries.summary: From data centers to Elon Musk funding to the AI lobby, the 2026 midterms are the most WIRED elections yet. These are the candidates we're following closely.
entries.content:
The midterm elections are a month away and the candidate pool has never been more WIRED. Races are being run—and likely decided—on Silicon Valley funding, data center debates, AI regulation, extremism, and more. From the contests that will decide the Senate to less attention-grabbing ones that will decide who controls voting in key swing states in 2028, these are the candidates and races we think are most worth watching closely in the weeks to come, and which we'll be keeping an eye on.

Former America PAC lawyer Chris Gober is running to represent Texas’ newly gerrymandered 10th district. Gober served as counsel for the Texas Republican congressional delegation for the 2025 redistricting effort that saw a new, gerrymandered map created for the 2026 midterms—one that was meant to create five new Republican congressional districts.

In addition to representing Musk’s PAC, Gober’s law firm, Lex Politica, has also represented Elevate New Mexico, a limited liability company that ran an advertising campaign supporting a controversial data center project in the state, as well as the Danube Institute USA, a think tank aligned with Hungary’s former right-wing leader Viktor Orban.

According to reporting from The New York Times, Gober was one of several lawyers who advised on the structure of the so-called Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in the weeks leading up to President Donald Trump’s inauguration.

The 10th district also includes Grimes County, where SpaceXAI and Tesla have said they plan to open a 100-million-square-foot “terafab” facility to manufacture semiconductors. In addition to his legal work, Gober’s LinkedIn lists him as general counsel for a lobbying group called Maven Advocacy Partners, the client base of which includes several defense tech startups. (Its name appears to be a reference to the Department of War’s Project Maven, which is supported by tech companies like Palantir and Anduril.) Gober also appears to run another company called Maven Defense Solutions. Both the company and the lobbying group share an address with his law firm, Lex Politica, and his campaign office.

Gober’s campaign has received $747,550 from the American Mission PAC, a right-leaning super PAC that has itself received funding from Leading the Future, a PAC focused on promoting AI-friendly candidates and policies. Leading the Future has raised over $140 million from Silicon Valley billionaires like OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Palantir cofounder Joe Lonsdale, as well as the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz.

This race will be the first in which someone directly involved with Musk and/or DOGE attempts to enter Congress.

A September poll showed Gober leading Rourk 48-41.

Former Pinal County sheriff Mark Lamb ran on a “God, family, freedom” platform and won the GOP primary in Arizona’s 5th congressional district with Trump’s endorsement. He also has ties to paramilitary groups, anti-immigration organizations, and the far-right constitutional sheriffs movement.

Though he may not self-identify as one, Lamb appeared to, at one time, be a constitutional sheriff who gained national notoriety for his refusal to enforce Covid restrictions. He has worked with the election-denial group True the Vote to get sheriffs to investigate elections and has also boosted the role of private militias. He even authorized the formation of a civilian posse while serving as sheriff of Pinal County, in response to Black Lives Matter protests in 2020. He regularly appears on right-wing podcasts, including those hosted by white nationalists and conspiracy theorists.

While sheriff, he was accused of sexual misconduct and racist remarks, though he has denied the allegations.

Arizona’s 5th District is solidly Republican, meaning Lamb is likely to become the first constitutional sheriff in Congress. Lamb will be the heavy favorite.

No polls available yet.

Before launching her congressional campaign, Democratic nominee Lauren Reinhold was a human resources administrator in the Social Security Administration. Like thousands of federal employees, she left her job in 2025 when DOGE and the Trump administration fired government workers, cut programs, and encouraged employees to resign en masse.

Now, she’s running for Congress in Kansas’ 1st district, which encompasses the mostly rural, western half of the state, against three-term incumbent Tracey Mann. The district has long been a Republican stronghold, and Reinhold faces an uphill battle. Though several former federal workers have attempted to run for office in the wake of DOGE’s mass firings of federal workers, Reinhold is one of few that have made it through the gauntlet of the Democratic primaries.

Her race may showcase whether the destruction that DOGE wrought in the first year of the Trump administration will be a real, long-term political liability for Republicans.

No polls available yet.

Democratic nominee for Wisconsin governor David Crowley will be facing off against Republican nominee and congressman Tom Tiffany, who has spent the past six years trying to undermine the democratic process in the US.

In December 2020, as a member of Congress, Tiffany signed up for a Texas lawsuit seeking to invalidate Joe Biden’s victory in the presidential election. He also voted against certifying the results in Pennsylvania and Arizona after the Capitol riot on January 6 and has suggested he would have overturned Wisconsin’s results. This year, he has warmly welcomed the FBI’s baseless investigation into the state’s elections.

If Tiffany wins, as governor he would have the power to appoint some of the state’s top officials on the Wisconsin Elections Commission, giving him the ability to install election deniers to oversee voting for the 2028 presidential election.

A Marquette Law School poll at the end of September found that Crowley led Tiffany by just 3 percentage points, 49-46.

Former Atlanta mayor and Democratic nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms and billionaire health care executive and Republican nominee Rick Jackson face a tight gubernatorial race in a pivotal swing state that has continued to be the focus of Trump’s false claims that the 2020 election was stolen.

Jackson has aligned himself with several of Trump’s agenda items. In ads run by his campaign during the primary, Jackson attacked immigrants, trans people, and DEI initiatives. He also ran ads attacking primary opponent and Georgia secretary of state Brad Raffensperger for refusing to cave to the Trump administration’s pressure to overturn the results of the 2020 election. Jackson has supported Republican efforts to redraw Georgia’s congressional map, which would eliminate majority-Black districts, thus favoring Republicans.

Jackson, who said he is invested in a data center in Texas, has also advocated against a moratorium on data centers, instead saying that local communities should choose for themselves whether to allow them.

Bottoms has said she would consider a moratorium and has made health care and expanding Medicaid central to her campaign.

Georgia will likely continue to be a central focus for the Trump administration, both as a place to relitigate the results of the 2020 election and as a critical swing state in 2028. Whoever wins the governor’s race here could determine the certification of future elections and the level to which the state participates in the administration’s national agenda, both with regards to issues like data centers and the erosion of trust in elections.

A recent Rasmussen Reports poll found that Jackson is leading Bottoms, 48-45 percent.

Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed is running against Republican nominee and former congressman Mike Rogers for Michigan’s crucial Senate seat.

Following a bruising primary, El-Sayed's main controversies have surrounded his criticisms of the war in Gaza and US military aid to Israel. This led to accusations he was too soft on antisemitism and too progressive a candidate for the general election. To secure the fractured Democratic base, El-Sayed has announced he will rally with former president Barack Obama in an effort to court Black voters, according to progressive operatives.

He has also sought to cast Rogers as the face of intrusive government surveillance, WIRED previously reported, at a time when voters have expressed privacy concerns around AI and Flock cameras.

Rogers has denied that characterization and, notably, has backed a one-year moratorium on new data center construction in the state, proactively taking steps to insulate himself from the other major tech issue on the trail.

Rogers, who has gone from refuting Trump’s election conspiracy theories to boosting them, has benefited from Elon Musk–affiliated America PAC funding, which has dumped more than $4 million into this race, mostly in negative ads against El-Sayed.

Michigan is a critical battleground state for both parties this midterm cycle because a path for Democrats to take the Senate majority largely rests on retaining this seat. If Democrats lose Michigan, they would need to flip a total of five Republican seats elsewhere.

A recent report from Hill/Emerson College Polling found that El-Sayed is leading Rogers by a narrow margin, 48-46 percent.

Republican nominee and entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy is running against Democratic nominee and Ohio’s former director of department of health Amy Acton in the state’s gubernatorial election.

So far, Big Tech has been bankrolling Ramaswamy’s campaign, through his super PAC. Elon Musk, Jeff Yass, and Bill Ackman have all donated in the millions. Ramaswamy, who was part of the early vision of Musk’s DOGE, has also been endorsed by Trump.

Besides his Silicon Valley bona fides (Ramaswamy’s view on data centers amount to

give everyone with a data center in their community “free electricity”), Ramaswamy has also espoused many of the Trump administration’s views on elections and other electoral policies. Ramaswamy has suggested that the January 6 attack on the Capitol was an “inside job” and, just this year, called on the Ohio legislature to add a constitutional amendment to the ballot that would enact restrictive voter-suppression measures. The governor of Ohio would be in a position to have more power over elections and could deeply impact the 2028 presidential election.

Polling suggests the race is extremely tight. A September poll from YouGov found that Acton maintains a slight lead over Ramaswamy, 48-45.

A number of secretary of state races across the country could heavily impact what happens for elections in 2028. In most states, the secretary of state is the chief election official; they run and certify elections, from county officials all the way up to the Senate. Now, a number of election deniers across the country are running for their state’s top election job.

In Nevada, Republican nominee Jim Marchant is running against Democratic nominee and current secretary of state Cisco Aguilar. Marchant, a former Nevada state representative, is an avowed election denier who was among the most ardent boosters of election denial in the wake of the 2020 election, going so far as to help arrange a QAnon-associated coalition of candidates for the 2022 midterms.

In 2022, Marchant lost out to Aguilar in the race for the secretary of state, but after winning the GOP primary in June, he’ll once again face Aguilar in November. Critically, Aguilar has stood up to efforts to undermine trust in elections over the course of the past four years, but the winner in November will oversee the 2028 presidential election in Nevada, a swing state that went for Biden in 2020 and Trump in 2024.

This race is a battle between one of the biggest boosters of election denial and one of the strongest defenders of election integrity.

No polls available yet.

While data centers have been a topic for voters across several key midterm races, nowhere is the debate more relevant than the Ohio Senate race.

Former senator and Democratic nominee Sherrod Brown is running against Republican nominee and former GOP lieutenant governor Jon Husted in one of the most contested races this election season. Husted, who has previously championed data center investments, has become a target statewide for his views.

Trump, who has endorsed Husted’s campaign, is adamantly pro–data center and went out of his way to express his opinions at a recent joint rally in Vandalia, Ohio. "We want them," Trump said. Husted’s campaign quickly issued a statement clarifying that Husted believed data centers were best left as a “local decision.”

Husted has been boosted by the Musk-affiliated America PAC, which has poured over $5 million into the Ohio Senate race, mainly in negative ads targeted at Brown, WIRED has previously reported. The only race in which Musk has spent more, according to federal campaign filings, has been the Senate race in Texas, a battleground state seen as a litmus test for Republicans this cycle.

Meanwhile, Fairshake, a super PAC funded by the crypto industry, is also planning to spend at least $30 million against Brown. (In 2024, when Brown lost his Senate reelection race, Fairshake spent $40 million against Brown, who then served as chair of the Senate Banking Committee and was a big crypto critic.)

According to a Bowling Green University poll, Brown leads Husted by three points, 48-45.

Texas has become a bellwether state for the midterms this November: If Democratic candidate James Talarico defeats attorney general Ken Paxton, the Democrats have a much better chance of taking the Senate majority.

The state has been ruby-red for decades, and Democrats would not have dreamed of this just months ago. But in a perfect storm, and with an unpopular Republican candidate besieged by scandal, Democrats have the best chance in decades of flipping the seat.

Recent approval polls put Paxton at negative 16, a number worse than every other Republican who is running in a close Senate race. Meanwhile, Talarico has been ahead in every public poll since mid-August.

The problem for Paxton is that he cannot exactly rely on Trump to boost his numbers, since the president is also experiencing negative approval ratings both in Texas and nationally. Paxton has been in lockstep with Trump for years, however. Paxton is an OG election denier, having led a failed multistate effort to overturn the 2020 results.

The silver lining for Paxton has been the colossal outside support that Republicans have marshaled to defend the seat. America PAC's biggest spending has focused on the race, pouring millions into defending the Republican’s seat.

Paxton isn’t universally beloved by Silicon Valley, however: Musk's SpaceX is suing Paxton in his role as state attorney general to stop information about its “terafab” operation being released under public records requests.

Talarico has maintained a narrow but consistent lead in polling; dating back to early June, he’s been ahead in all but two of 24 polls tracked by Silver Bulletin.

Republican nominee Riley Owen is running against Democratic nominee Ben McAdams for Utah’s 1st congressional district. Owen briefly served as a White House policy analyst during the first Trump administration and later worked for a startup using drones for conservation efforts. McAdams served as the representative for the state’s 4th Congressional district between 2019 and 2021 but lost to current representative Burgess Owens.

This little-known race has some fascinating funding implications: McAdams has received $1,128,697.73 in donations from Think Big, a PAC that describes itself as supporting “Democratic candidates dedicated to advancing AI innovation in America.” Think Big, in turn, is financed by Leading the Future.

McAdams also has a small stake in a data center project being built in rural Utah that, when completed, is expected to have a much larger power capacity than a controversial nearby project in Box Elder County.

No polls available yet.
